What this page practises

  • I can state Newton's third law and name the reaction force.
  • I can explain how a rocket launches, using Newton's third law.
  • I can calculate weight with W = mg.
  • I can calculate the unbalanced force, then the acceleration with F = ma.
  • I can show and name the forces on a rocket.
  • I can explain why a rocket's acceleration changes.

Warm-up

Say it the exam way

At launch, the rocket pushes the exhaust gases . The exhaust gases push the rocket . This is Newton's law.

On a force diagram, the upward force is the and the downward force is the . The unbalanced force is thrust weight.

As fuel is used, the mass . The weight falls, so the unbalanced force and the acceleration .

Answers

Say it the exam way

(1) down · (2) up · (3) third · (4) engine thrust · (5) weight · (6) minus · (7) decreases · (8) increases · (9) increases

2026 Section 1, Question 6: answer D

  • A Not this one. I is right, but II is right too. As the mass falls, the weight falls, so the unbalanced force (thrust − weight) increases.
  • B Not this one. II is right, but so is I. Less mass means more acceleration for the same force (a = F ÷ m).
  • C Not this one. III is wrong. The exhaust gases push the rocket up. The force pair is the rocket and the gases, not the gases and the Earth.
  • D Right. I and II are both true: the mass decreases and the unbalanced force increases, so the acceleration increases. III is wrong: the gases push the rocket up (Newton's third law).
  • E Not this one. III is wrong. The rocket is pushed up by the exhaust gases, not by the gases pushing on the Earth.

2022 Section 1, Question 4: answer B

  • A Not this one. Once the rocket leaves the ground there is no ground force. The pair is between the rocket and the water.
  • B Right. Newton's third law: the rocket pushes the water down, and the water pushes the rocket up.
  • C Not this one. This pair acts on the water and the ground, not on the rocket.
  • D Not this one. The water does not need to push on the ground. The rocket is pushed by the water it throws out.
  • E Not this one. Losing water does reduce the weight, but that is not what makes the rocket launch. Look for the force pair.

2022 Section 1, Question 9: answer A

  • A Right. R and S push gas forwards (to the right). The gas pushes the spacecraft back (to the left), against its motion, so it slows down.
  • B Not this one. Q pushes the spacecraft forwards and S pushes it backwards. The forces cancel.
  • C Not this one. P and Q push gas backwards, so the gas pushes the spacecraft forwards. It speeds up.
  • D Not this one. P and R push in opposite directions. The forces cancel.
  • E Not this one. All four push equally in opposite directions. The forces are balanced, so the speed does not change.

2017 Section 1, Question 17: answer D

  • A Not this one. g on Mars (3.7 N kg−1) is less than on Earth (9.8 N kg−1), so the weight on Mars is less.
  • B Not this one. Weight is W = mg, and g is different on Mars.
  • C Not this one. Same mass, but g is smaller on Mars, so the weight is less.
  • D Right. W = mg and g is smaller on Mars, so the weight is less. Unbalanced force = thrust − weight. Same thrust, less weight, so the unbalanced force is greater.
  • E Not this one. The weight is less, but work out thrust − weight. A smaller weight leaves a greater unbalanced force.

2014 Section 1, Question 18: answer E

  • A Not this one. True, but a constant g does not explain a constant speed. A constant speed needs balanced forces.
  • B Not this one. Where it came from does not matter. Look at the forces acting on it now.
  • C Not this one. If air resistance were bigger than the weight, the unbalanced force would be upwards and the spacecraft would slow down.
  • D Not this one. Then the unbalanced force is downwards and the spacecraft speeds up.
  • E Right. The forces are balanced, so the speed stays constant (Newton's first law).
